avr: Campaign site lists 'voting rights' among measures he has signed (2026); no new AVR or voting-rights proposal named.

meddebt: His 26-point 'Workers First' agenda would cancel medical debt (2026).
priorauth: Health plan backs a bipartisan prior-authorization reform, including barring AI-only denials (2026); reform, not elimination.
mental: Education plan would prioritize student mental health by adding school counselors statewide (2026).
datactr: Would pause new data center tax abatements pending audits and make data centers pay for their own power and grid upgrades (2026).

renter: Would cap security deposits at one month's rent and ban junk rental fees (2026).

workforce: Workers First plan would partner with unions to expand registered apprenticeships, enrolling 50% more apprentices (Jun 2026).

childcare: Education plan would expand pre-K access to more families (2026); no broader child care subsidy plan, so related only.
vouchers: Opposes public money for private schools and wants K-12 per-pupil funding raised to the national average (May 2026).
college: Education plan would limit tuition increases at Nevada colleges and restore state higher-ed funding to peer-state levels (2026).
ai: Education plan backs limits on social media's addictive features for kids, stronger platform safety standards for minors, and a student-data sale ban (2026).
safety: Pledged a permanent budget line for domestic-violence victim services and a statewide 911-to-sentencing case-tracking system (Sep 2026).
guard: As attorney general, called the Los Angeles federalization unlawful and joined multistate briefs; opposed Nevada Guard support for ICE (2025).
tariff: Pledges to "stand up to tariffs" raising housing costs and pursue legal action against them; faults Lombardo's tariff support (2026).
fraud: Pledges to root out fraud, waste, and abuse and let Medicaid open fraud probes on its own (2026); no inspector general proposal.
wage: As Senate majority leader he advanced a 2017 minimum wage hike bill that was vetoed (cited Jun 2026); no $15 pledge found.
house: Housing plan would cut permitting red tape, set statewide housing goals and standards, and open ~10,000 vacant acres to building (2026).
roe: Supports enshrining abortion rights through 24 weeks in the Nevada Constitution (Aug 2026).
pfml: Sponsored a 2017 paid sick leave expansion (vetoed); campaign signaled support for expanding it (Jun 2026). Sick leave, not a PFML program.
avr: Opposes a photo voter ID requirement, citing no evidence of fraud (Aug 2026); not an AVR or state voting rights act pledge.

clean: His Cabinet backed bills to change, not meet, Vermont's climate requirements (Mar 2026); he vetoed a faster renewable-purchase bill (2024) and wants to slow targets.
ptax: In his State of the State asked lawmakers for some short-term property tax relief while pursuing Act 73 education reform (Jan 2026).

teacher: Touts Act 73 education reform as raising pay for teachers paid less than peers in wealthier districts, a narrower step (Jan 2026).
safety: FY27 budget proposes $500,000 for a new accountability court for repeat offenders (Jan 2026); narrow, not police hiring or violence intervention.
ice: Signed a 2017 law limiting Vermont police involvement in federal immigration enforcement; related, not sensitive-location rules (2017).
guard: Turned down Trump's requests for Vermont troops and called the Chicago and Portland deployments unconstitutional (Oct 2025).
tariff: Called the Trump administration's new Canada tariffs 'simply a bad idea' that will raise costs on Vermonters (Jul 2026).
fraud: Created a Government Modernization and Efficiency Team for efficiency audits and in 2026 urged tech systems to cut fraud and waste (Jan 2026).
wage: Vetoed S.40, which would have raised Vermont's minimum wage to $15 by 2024, preferring the existing inflation-indexed system (May 2018).
house: Signed S.100, the HOME Act, easing municipal zoning and Act 250 rules statewide to allow more housing (Jun 2023).
roe: Signed a broad law codifying abortion rights (Jun 2019) and backed the 2022 Prop 5 constitutional amendment protecting reproductive liberty (2022).
pfml: Vetoed mandatory paid leave bills H.196 (May 2018) and H.107 (Jan 2020; override failed by one vote), offering a voluntary state-employee-based plan instead.

drugbd: Vetoed the bill creating a prescription drug affordability board with upper payment limits, after trying to make it a study panel (May 2026).
meddebt: Would keep people from falling into medical debt after one emergency (2026).
priorauth: Signed HB736 limiting insurers' prior authorization requirements to prevent care delays; narrower than ending it, no insulin cap found (Apr 2026).
mental: Signed HB957 on 988 crisis-line information in schools (Apr 2026) and HB 248/SB 317 joint behavioral-health crisis response (Apr 2026); no major funding found.
datactr: Says high energy users must pay their fair share and pressed PJM on it, but opposed an early end to data centers' tax break and cut a cost-shift provision (Jan-Apr 2026).
utility: Proposed capping Dominion's profit at 9.3% with excess credited to customers (rejected) and signed utility billing/disconnect protections (Apr 2026).
clean: Signed HB 1393/SB 253 expanding weatherization and energy aid and a package creating the Virginia Clean Energy Innovation Bank (May 2026).
downpay: Signed HB164/SB328 removing caps on employer-assisted homeownership grants; narrower than general down payment aid (Apr 2026).
renter: Proposed extending the eviction response window to two weeks and signed HB15/SB48 tenant protections (Jan-Apr 2026).
workforce: Signed SB592 aligning career and technical education with workforce needs and bills to add CTE teachers (Apr 2026); not an apprenticeship expansion.
schools: Biennial budget she signed carries a record $2 billion in new public education funding (Jul 2026).
childcare: Called for expanding access to Virginia's child care subsidy program, short of universal care (Jan 2026).
teacher: Told the General Assembly Virginia must pay teachers more, 'Period.' (Jan 2026).
ai: Signed SB108 bell-to-bell school phone ban and SB568 device-addiction instruction (Apr 2026); kids' screen limits, not AI or platform rules.
gun: Signed SB 749/HB 217 barring sales of certain assault-style firearms and magazines over 15 rounds (May 2026), plus ghost-gun and domestic-abuser bans (Apr 2026).
ice: Signed SB491 limiting sharing of student immigration data with DHS absent a judicial warrant; amended mask limits on agents (Apr 2026).
guard: Signed SB 337 (Apr 2026), which orders a study of how Virginia should respond to Guard deployments the governor hasn't approved and bars using the Guard to intimidate voters.
tariff: Statement says Trump's 'reckless tariffs' raised costs for Virginia families and farmers and urged no new trade war (Feb 2026).
npv: Signed HB965 joining the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (Apr 2026).
wage: Signed HB1/SB1 raising Virginia's minimum wage to $13.75 in 2027 and $15 in 2028 (Apr 2026).
house: Signed SB531 requiring localities statewide to allow accessory dwelling units and capping ADU permit costs (Apr 2026).
roe: Told lawmakers she supports the constitutional amendment protecting reproductive freedom; also signed a right-to-contraception law (Jan-Apr 2026).
pfml: Proposed a statewide paid family and medical leave program; her amendments to SB2/HB1207 were accepted and it became law (Apr 2026).

clean: Supplemental budgets add $30M for Tribal clean energy projects and $30M for home energy bill aid (Apr 2026); no new clean-power standard.

gun: Signed HB 1163 requiring a state permit and safety training to buy a gun (May 2025).

fraud: Executive order created a chief fraud prevention officer and statewide fraud workgroup; plans a state False Claims Act (Oct 2026).

pubopt: 'Badger Basics' opens BadgerCare as a public option for every household (Apr 2026).
mental: Badger Basics would build a statewide No Wrong Door mental health system with navigators in all 72 counties (Apr 2026).
datactr: Data centers must 'pay the full cost of grid upgrades they drive'; would sign a repeal of their sales-tax break (2026).
utility: Says he will first focus on lowering utility costs (Nov 2026) and pledged to cut energy bills (Apr 2026); no rate freeze, cap, or utility-accountability plan named.
clean: Badger Basics pledges to cut energy bills for families and renters, and he wants data centers on 100% renewable energy (Apr-Oct 2026); no clean-power standard named.

workforce: Badger Basics would expand dual enrollment and apprenticeship programs (Apr 2026); repeated apprenticeship pledge after winning (Nov 2026).
schools: First-30-days plan pledges to close the special education funding gap so districts aren't forced to cut programs (Mar 2026).
prek: First-30-days plan pledges to pass universal pre-K using existing providers (Mar 2026).
childcare: Would cap out-of-pocket child care costs at 7% of income for all families (2026).
vouchers: Would fully fund public schools (2026); no stated plan on Wisconsin's voucher programs.
safety: First-30-days plan pledges to strengthen and fund domestic violence prevention and crisis support (Mar 2026); narrower than broad police or violence-intervention funding.

guard: No statement found on federal Guard deployments.
tariff: Attacked opponent Tiffany for backing Trump's 'tariff taxes' and not standing up for farmers and manufacturers (Aug 2026).
wage: Badger Basics would raise the minimum wage to $15 immediately and $20 by 2030 (Apr 2026).
house: Badger Basics would build more housing statewide through zoning flexibility and adaptive reuse (Apr 2026).
roe: Says abortion must be 'protected at all costs' (2026).
pfml: His campaign plan's child care system explicitly includes paid family leave (2026); as county executive he signed paid parental leave for county workers (Apr 2022).

medicaid: Would fully fund the Medicaid rebase, $319 million plus $728 million (2026).
mental: FY2026-27 budget invests in the behavioral-health workforce and adds two state psychiatric hospital units (Apr 2026).
rural: 2025-27 budget proposal calls for "supporting rural clinics" (Mar 2025); no rural-hospital funding named.
datactr: Spokesperson said Stein has long held that data centers must pay their own way so families don't foot the bill (May 2026).
utility: Vetoed SB 266, warning it could cost ratepayers up to $23 billion through 2050 (Jul 2025); no rate freeze or cap.
clean: Vetoed SB 266, which scrapped Duke Energy's 2030 carbon-cut goal, saying it could cost ratepayers up to $23 billion (Jul 2025).
mctax: Budget would raise the standard deduction to $26,500 while pausing scheduled income tax rate cuts (Apr 2026).
workforce: FY2026-27 budget proposes $448M+ for opportunity programs incl. NC Career Launch youth apprenticeships (Apr 2026).
schools: FY2026-27 budget proposes ~$2.3 billion for educators, student outcomes, and child care, raising starting teacher pay to highest in the Southeast (Apr 2026).
prek: Budget includes new investment in NC Pre-K, but no universal pre-K pledge (Apr 2026).
childcare: Would raise child care subsidy rates and set a statewide floor (2026).
teacher: Average 11% teacher raise, highest starting pay in the Southeast (Apr 2026 budget).
vouchers: Would phase out the universal Opportunity Scholarship voucher expansion (Apr 2026 budget).
college: FY2026-27 budget funds free community college tuition for short-term workforce credentials (Apr 2026); narrower than free degree programs.
ai: 2025-27 budget proposal aims to reduce "the distraction of cell phones in classrooms" (Mar 2025); no social media or AI rules.
safety: FY2026-27 budget proposes a 5% law-enforcement raise atop 10% earlier, a Fentanyl Control Unit, and more school security (Apr 2026).
gun: Vetoed SB 50 permitless carry, saying it "makes North Carolinians less safe" (Jun 2025); blocked a loosening, no new gun law.
ice: Vetoed HB 318 and SB 153, which expanded state cooperation with ICE (Jun 2025); not a sensitive-locations rule, and he backs ICE alerts for serious crimes.
guard: Signed the Aug 2025 Democratic governors' statement against deployments without consent; sent one Guard member to D.C. for America 250 (2026).
house: 2025-27 budget proposal includes "building more homes" for families facing high costs (Mar 2025); no zoning or permitting plan given.

ss.name: Texas
ss.rule: Final passage takes a majority of senators present; the lieutenant governor breaks ties. Under the Senate's current rules a bill can't reach the floor without 5/9 of members (18 of 31) agreeing to take it up, and the Republican majority writes the rules for 2027, including how much agenda power Goodwin keeps.

medicaid: Says she will push the Legislature to expand Medicaid, mostly federally funded, and strengthen rural hospitals (Jun and Nov 2026).
pubopt: Says she will push to expand Medicaid and ensure every Texas child has affordable care (Jun-Nov 2026); related to, not a public option or universal plan.
priorauth: Would ban insurers' bad-faith coverage denials, a related but narrower step than ending prior authorization; no insulin co-pay plan found (2026).
rural: Campaign promised to strengthen rural hospitals, alongside a push to expand Medicaid (Nov 2026 recap).
datactr: Would end over $1 billion in data center tax exemptions and impose a permit moratorium (2026).
utility: Would freeze electricity rates (Oct 2026) and hold down utility costs by making industry pay its fair share (Jun 2026).
renter: Platform would hold landlords accountable for AI-driven rent pricing and rent hikes without notice; she also backs cash back for renters (Jan 2026).
ptax: Commits to cutting homeowner property taxes and ultimately eliminating residential property taxes, plus cash back for renters (2026).
mctax: Candidate questionnaire says she would cut taxes for families and small businesses, without a specific income-tax mechanism (2026).
schools: Pledges to 'save' public schools by moving money to teacher pay, smaller classes, and special education, and to end vouchers (Oct 2026).
vouchers: Pledges to end private-school vouchers and stop state takeovers of districts (2026).
safety: Would shift Operation Lone Star money toward local public safety (Jun 2026) and spend 'the money it takes to keep our community safe' (Nov 2026); no specific program.
ice: Opposed forcing local police to help enforce immigration law (2017) and criticizes federal ICE tactics; related, not sensitive-location rules (2026).
guard: Criticized Abbott for sending Texas Guard troops to Chicago and Portland as 'political theater' (Oct 2025).
fraud: Pledges to audit and cancel corrupt vendor contracts and end no-bid contracts, narrower than an inspector general overhaul (2026).
house: 'Expand the supply of homes Texans can afford' (2026).
roe: On the Roe anniversary she vowed to end Texas's abortion ban and guarantee women's right to privacy and care as governor (Jan 2026).

ss.rule: Georgia's constitution requires a majority of all 56 senators (29) for final passage, whoever is absent. The lieutenant governor presides but casts no tie-breaking vote on bills.

why.fil: Changing the rule by precedent (the 'nuclear option') needs a simple majority. At 50–50, VP Vance breaks the tie against it, so 51 is the real number.
why.sch: Decided by secret ballot inside the Democratic caucus in early December. Schumer needs a simple majority of caucus members; Republicans don't vote.
why.isr: Arms-sale disapproval resolutions are privileged under the Arms Export Control Act, so they can't be filibustered: 51 passes the Senate. Trump would veto, which takes 67 to override.
why.iran: War Powers Act joint resolutions get expedited, filibuster-proof votes, so 51 passes the Senate. Trump would veto, which takes 67 to override.
why.tariff: Resolutions ending a national emergency under the National Emergencies Act are privileged, so ending the tariff emergencies takes 51. The Trade Review Act itself is an ordinary bill (60 while the filibuster stands). Trump would veto either; 67 overrides.

Would end the $38 million data center tax exemption and charge them families' water rate (2026).

Calls for a moratorium on new data centers until they pay their own way up front (2026 climate plan).
Campaign plan: data centers must bear their added energy costs, get no tax breaks, and face a moratorium until rules exist (2026).
Would pause new data center tax abatements pending audits and make data centers pay for their own power and grid upgrades (2026).
Would require data centers to 'pay their fair share' and generate their own power (2026).
Would require data centers to pay extra utility and environmental costs (Apr 2026).
Would end over $1 billion in data center tax exemptions and impose a permit moratorium (2026).
Data centers must 'pay the full cost of grid upgrades they drive'; would sign a repeal of their sales-tax break (2026).

utility.ev: Signed a cap on Delmarva's recovery of nonessential infrastructure spending plus required PSC audits of utilities (Aug 2026), after attacking Delmarva overcharging (Jan 2026).
Playbook pledges to extend the utility base-rate freeze (Oct 2026).
Would declare a state of emergency 'to freeze insurance and utility rates' and crack down on price gouging (2026 voter guide).

Would make utilities justify every line on bills and buy power at the lowest price (2026).
Would restrict utilities from using campaign contributions to influence regulators (2026).
Would restore efficiency programs cut in the HB 6 bribery scandal and appoint regulators 'not beholden to utility companies' (2026).
Energy plan would have the state audit Rhode Island Energy to make sure proposed rate increases are justified (Apr 2026); no rate freeze.
Would freeze electricity rates (Oct 2026) and hold down utility costs by making industry pay its fair share (Jun 2026).

Signed HB 304, putting $50M a year into a property tax reduction fund and $50M into school bond/levy relief (Mar 2025).
Proposed and signed doubling the senior circuit breaker credit for high property taxes/rent to $2,400 (2023 tax law, Oct 2023).
Signed HB 594, raising the senior property-tax 'circuit breaker' credit from $1,000 to $1,550 for homeowners, indexed to CPI (Jul 2025).
Signed SB 542 and HB 231 creating a lower Homestead Rate for primary residences and long-term rentals plus up to $400 rebates (2025; touted Nov 2025).
Signed HB 1176, raising the primary-residence property tax credit from $500 to $1,600 a year, funded by Legacy Fund earnings (May 2025).
Budget targets $4.2 billion in property-tax relief at those most in need (Mar 2026).
Signed the 2023 expansion of the Property Tax/Rent Rebate program for seniors and people with disabilities (2023).
Proposed and signed SB 96 (county half-cent sales tax to cut owner-occupied property taxes) and SB 245 (homeowner property tax reduction fund), plus senior refunds (Mar 2026).
Proposes freezing property-tax increases on senior-occupied homes, worked out with counties (Oct 2026).
Feb 2026 agenda cuts residential assessment rate from 11.5% to 9% and widens homestead exemption for seniors and disabled veterans.
Would double the homestead exemption from $25,000 to $50,000 and deepen the Property Tax Fairness Credit (2026).
Campaign site would eliminate property taxes on seniors' and veterans' homesteads, with a voter-approved senior exemption (May 2026).
Campaign platform would reduce and eliminate personal property taxes, including the car tax, for seniors and veterans (2026).
Day after winning, pledged 'meaningful property tax relief' as a first-term priority (Nov 2026).

workforce.ev: Signed budget funding 75 teacher apprentices a year and ending licensing fees for nurses and the trades (May 2026).
Signed the RAISE Act expanding registered apprenticeships and creating an apprenticeship office (Apr 2025).
Proposed $15M new for career and technical education centers and a Workforce of the Future Challenge, EO 25-16 (Jan 2025).

State of the State proposed expanding training for nurses and physician assistants (Jan 2026).
LaunchPad Florida plan would link high schools, community colleges, and employers for paid apprenticeships in construction, manufacturing, defense (Nov 2026).
2026 plan: work experience or apprenticeship for every young Mainer by 20, expand registered apprenticeships, and CTE.

Health workforce plan would double apprenticeships from 5,000 to 10,000 and scale career pipelines (Aug 2026).

Pledges to create workforce training programs for students and expand workforce development and skills training (Jul 2026).
Would expand career-tech programs for jobs without a 4-year degree, citing a 7,500-student waitlist for nursing and welding (Sep 2026).
Proposes a $100M career and technical education bond, trades training, and more CCRI capacity for adult learners (May 2026).
Badger Basics would expand dual enrollment and apprenticeship programs (Apr 2026); repeated apprenticeship pledge after winning (Nov 2026).
Jan 2026 State of the State proposes a Workforce Readiness & Opportunity Act to expand micro-credentials and portable benefits, plus more workforce-training money.

prek.ev: Touts expanding preschool and the state's largest early childhood investment; FY27 budget proposed $748 million for the Early Childhood Block Grant (Feb 2026).
Pledges to fully fund First Class Pre-K, aiming for a seat for every family that wants one in his first term (Oct 2026).
Pledges to support and expand Colorado's Universal Preschool program (2026 campaign).
Proposes universal pre-K in every Gateway City (2026).
Education plan (June 2026) would offer free full-day pre-K to every Maine 4-year-old whose family wants it.
Would expand free pre-K to all 3- and 4-year-olds (May 2026 education plan).
Campaign plan pledges a pathway to universal preschool statewide (2026).
Would 'ensure every Rhode Island family has access to pre-Kindergarten' (2026).
First-30-days plan pledges to pass universal pre-K using existing providers (Mar 2026).

safety.ev: Would 'fully fund' Prop 36, including court-ordered drug treatment for defendants (2026 voter guide).
Signed law formally establishing the Office of Gun Violence Prevention and Community Safety he first created by order in 2025 (Sep 2026).
Jan 2025 State of the State proposed $7M for Highway Patrol pay, $6.5M for corrections officers and 500 more prison beds.
FY2027 budget proposes $352 million for gun violence prevention and expands Crime Analysis Centers statewide (Jan 2026).
Signed HB 2015 creating $100 million in grants for local police hiring and other public safety (May 2025).
Called funding troopers and Village Public Safety Officers 'a core state responsibility' and pledged to build on VPSO gains (Jul 2026).
Playbook proposes more state troopers, a statewide gang unit, and a Safe Streets Act on violent offenders (Oct 2026).
Re-election launch pledged to 'raise pay for law enforcement and firefighters' (Oct 2025).
Blueprint pledges to recruit and invest in police and sheriffs and fund co-responders for mental health crises (May 2026).
Campaign plan offers hiring bonuses and competitive pay to recruit police officers, plus firm sentences for violent offenders (Nov 2026).
Campaign platform: expand GBI investigative help for smaller police departments and invest in 'targeted violence reduction efforts' (2026).
Touts historic law enforcement and public safety funding and a 44% homicide drop; pledged a 'public safety turnaround' (2026).
Pledges police and first responders 'have the resources they need' and to expand police recruiting pipelines (Oct 2026).
FY2026-27 budget proposes a 5% law-enforcement raise atop 10% earlier, a Fentanyl Control Unit, and more school security (Apr 2026).
May 2026 plan: tools and tech for police to arrest violent offenders, plus afterschool and mentorship programs to "prevent crime."
Pledged a permanent budget line for domestic-violence victim services and a statewide 911-to-sentencing case-tracking system (Sep 2026).
Campaign pledges to "fully fund the police and public safety" and rebuild state-local partnerships (Jul 2026); no violence-intervention detail.
Education plan would keep expanding School Resource Officer programs; priorities pledge to work with law enforcement and toughen violent-crime penalties (Aug 2026).

fraud.ev: Proposes agency audits, independently verified savings, and stepped-up Medicaid fraud enforcement (Oct 2026).
Would restore the full powers of the state Auditor to find misspent tax dollars and require annual audits of the voucher program (2026 campaign).
Proposed 40-plus anti-fraud changes, including surprise audits and a statewide inspector general (May 2026).
Campaign platform pledges a comprehensive audit of state and local governments to root out fraud and waste (2026).

clean.ev: Signed SB 25, Clean, and Reliable Grid Affordability Act, boosting battery storage, virtual power plants, and utility efficiency (Jan 2026).
Vetoed SB 266, which scrapped Duke Energy's 2030 carbon-cut goal, saying it could cost ratepayers up to $23 billion (Jul 2025).
Expanded Community Solar to 3,000 MW, fast-tracked battery storage, and approved new solar and battery projects (Jan-Apr 2026).
Signed HB 1393/SB 253 expanding weatherization and energy aid and a package creating the Virginia Clean Energy Innovation Bank (May 2026).
Official statement pledges lower electric bills by building cheap, clean renewable energy (Jun 2026).
Blueprint backs solar and wind statewide, a Geothermal Development Authority, and meeting Colorado's emission goals (May 2026).
Campaign pledges a '100% zero-carbon grid by 2040' and more solar, wind, geothermal, and heat pumps (2026).
2026 plan: 'Deliver 100% clean energy by 2040,' regular auctions for solar, wind, and storage, expanded heat pump programs.
May 2026 plan would lower utility costs by "doubling down on renewable energy."
Pledges to expand residential and utility-scale solar and make Nevada "a global clean energy leader to lower costs" (Jun 2026).
Affordability plan backs more power from the lowest-cost and cleanest sources and would restore efficiency programs cut by HB 6 (Apr 2026).
Budget address pushes his Lightning Plan to build in-state generation, speed siting, and add more renewables (Feb 2026).
Energy plan commits $40M for home and small-business solar and batteries, solar on 250 public buildings, and more wind (Apr 2026).

teacher.ev: Signed the LEARNS Act, which raised the minimum starting teacher salary (Mar 2023).
Signed HB 1890 (Act 233) setting salary step and longevity raises for educators (Jul 2026).
Campaign credits him with quadrupling Illinois's minimum teacher salary (to $40,000 under a 2019 law) (2026).
Jan 2026 budget proposed $159 million for mandatory educator raises, nearly 7% take-home.
Signed Dec 2024 law to make a $2,000 teacher raise permanent (voided when voters rejected Amendment 2); pushed new stipends in 2026.
Signed and touts the 2021 TEACH Act, which pays districts incentives to raise starting teacher salaries (cited Oct 2024).
Platform pledges to raise teacher pay to attract top educators and to create a defined-benefit retirement system (2026).
Education plan pledges livable teacher wages so teachers need not work multiple jobs (2026 campaign).
Would raise average starting teacher pay from $48,000 to $60,000 and end state income tax for teachers (Aug-Sept 2026).
Would expedite raising teacher minimum starting pay to $50,000 (June 2026 education plan).
Would require starting teacher salaries of at least $60,000 (2026).
Proposed teacher pay raises in his budget (Nov 2021); the 2022 teacher raise law followed.
Education plan would raise minimum pay for all education staff to an inflation-indexed living wage (Jan 2026).
Campaign site pledges to make Oklahoma teacher pay tops in the region, tied to performance (May 2026).

house.ev: Signed bipartisan bills requiring larger cities to allow casitas and middle housing like duplexes (May 2024).
Signed HB 8002 easing parking mandates and requiring town housing growth plans (Nov 2025), after vetoing the broader HB 5002 (June 2025).
Said he backs Rep. Doug Miller's bill to cut regulatory barriers to homebuilding '100%' (Jan 2026) and signed HEA 1001 on housing (Mar 2026).
Jan 2026 budget proposes $150 million for the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, which he says would leverage about $1B in new housing.
Cut environmental approvals for housing from over a year to 30 days (2026).
Signed 2023 pro-housing zoning laws forcing big cities to allow duplexes and backyard units, dubbed the "Montana Miracle" (cited Oct 2024).
Jan 2025 executive budget proposed nearly $105M for housing supply and affordability, including a $50M public-private housing program.
Signed 2025 laws setting a 60-day local permitting clock, expanding ADUs and allowing business-to-housing conversions; called housing her top priority (2026 State of the State).
Signed SB 1537 (Mar 2024), allowing one-time urban growth boundary expansions and creating a housing accountability office.
Signed SB531 requiring localities statewide to allow accessory dwelling units and capping ADU permit costs (Apr 2026).
Signed S.100, the HOME Act, easing municipal zoning and Act 250 rules statewide to allow more housing (Jun 2023).
Signed supplemental budgets he called the largest state-funded housing investment of any supplemental, incl. $123M Housing Trust Fund (Apr 2026).
Would 'cut red tape that gets in the way of building more homes' and open state land for housing (2026).
Plans to build 21,000 homes by 2030 by easing duplexes, quadplexes, and ADUs and simplifying permitting and inspections (2026 campaign).
Proposed statewide zoning standards limiting local control over housing types (Feb 2026).
Affordability agenda would revamp zoning, set a statewide shot clock auto-approving stalled projects, and pause new housing codes (Feb 2026).
Housing Action Plan would modernize the Municipalities Planning Code to ease residential building and speed permits (Feb 2026).
Housing plan targets 20,000 new units in eight years via a builder loan fund and modular-construction incentives (Mar 2026).
Governor-elect plans to simplify housing permitting and regulation and build workforce housing on unused government land via public-private deals (Nov 2026).

His state program with a nonprofit has erased medical debt for hundreds of thousands; announced 97,000 more residents in June 2026.

Signed the Fair Medical Debt Reporting Act keeping medical debt off New Yorkers' credit reports (Dec 2023).
Signed SB 605 barring medical debt from consumer credit reports (Sept 2025).
Signed SB 5480 barring medical debt from credit reports (Apr 2025), calling medical debt a huge issue nationwide.

Would ban medical debt from credit reports (2026).
His 26-point 'Workers First' agenda would cancel medical debt (2026).

priorauth.ev: Signed the Healthcare Protection Act banning prior authorization for in-patient mental health care (2024).
Would eliminate prior authorization: 'if your doctor says you need it, you'll get it' (2026 address).

ai.ev: Signed SB 612 letting parents sue social media firms whose content harms minors, up to $10,000 per violation (Apr 2025).

Signed HB 1126, the Walker Montgomery Protecting Children Online Act: parental consent for minors' social media accounts (May 2024).

Executive Order 6 created an Office of Youth Online Mental Health Safety and Awareness; budget adds a Social Media Research Center (Mar-Apr 2026).

Kids' tech safety plan: ban social media for under-16s, app-store age verification, no sale of minors' data (Jul 2026).

Budget address proposes age verification and parental consent for AI companion bots and a school cellphone ban (Feb 2026).
Lead sponsor of the Kids Online Safety Act, S.1748, reintroduced in 2025; pressed Congress to pass it (Dec 2025). Federal bill, not a state plan.
Has made AI regulation a major agenda item and says it is 'the states' job to protect children' from AI harms, despite White House pushback (2026).

Signed HB 54 creating a statewide Office of Suicide Prevention (Aug 2025).

2026 plan: fully staff crisis hotlines, crisis receiving centers, mobile crisis teams, more school mental health staff.

May 2026 plan pledges investment in mental health and addiction programs and an Office of Community Safety for behavioral-health crises.

Jan 2026 State of the State proposed expanding "elite mental health units" for people in crisis and youth online mental-health protections.
Safety plan pledges to invest in addiction treatment and mental health services statewide (Jul 2026); no crisis-line detail.

Signed SB 611 (July 2023) tightening Oregon's cap on annual rent increases.

Campaign platform commits to policies stopping large corporations from buying up homes en masse (2026 campaign, CalMatters voter guide).

Would crack down on corporate single-family landlords (2026).
Would ban landlords from using AI pricing algorithms to fix and raise rents (2026 campaign).
Housing plan: temporary 100-day ban on private equity home buying; crack down on corporate investors raising rents (2026).
Housing plan would ban algorithmic rent-price coordination and bar landlords from rejecting voucher holders (2026).

renter.ev: Would ban rent-fixing, including landlords' use of AI pricing (2026).
Would cap security deposits at one month's rent and ban junk rental fees (2026).

Platform would hold landlords accountable for AI-driven rent pricing and rent hikes without notice; she also backs cash back for renters (Jan 2026).

pubopt.ev: Health plan pledges to build on the Colorado Option public plan to offer cheaper individual and family coverage (2026 campaign).
Would 'create a public health insurance option: a state-backed plan' (2026).
Health plan pledges to drive enrollment in Battle Born State Plans, Nevada's new public option, with an outreach campaign (2026).

downpay.ev: Proposed new down payment assistance funding (Feb 2026).
Housing plan would expand down payment assistance for first-time buyers, including teachers and essential workers (2026 campaign).

Would expand $25,000 down payment assistance and ban broker fees (2026).
2026 campaign plan pledges to boost starter homes and down payment assistance for first-time buyers; no broker-fee stance.

Campaign blueprint explicitly opposes introducing voucher programs and notes he opposed Amendment 80, the school-choice measure (May 2026).
Would phase out the universal Opportunity Scholarship voucher expansion (Apr 2026 budget).
Pledges to end private-school vouchers and stop state takeovers of districts (2026).

gun.ev: Campaign site lists 'gun violence prevention measures' among laws he has signed (2026).
Signed laws licensing gun dealers, registering ghost guns and creating an Office of Gun Violence Prevention (Sep 2026).
Signed SB 1230 (Act 52), barring guns in sensitive places and requiring secure storage in vehicles (Jun 2023).
Signed SB 8, the Safe Gun Storage Act, and HB 1373 requiring crime-gun tracing (Jul 2025).
Vetoed HB 312 (concealed carry at 18-20) and HB 78 (gun-seller liability shield) in Apr 2026; both overridden. Backed a red-flag-style law in 2023.
Signed Chapter 135 gun law (ghost guns, red flag) Jul 2024 and backs keeping it via Yes on Question 9 (Oct 2026).
Signed SB 334 restricting sale of machine-gun-convertible pistols, facing NRA suit (May 26 2026).

Signed HB 1163 requiring a state permit and safety training to buy a gun (May 2025).
Blueprint pledges to 'sign, support, and defend' responsible gun safety laws (May 2026).
Campaign platform: will 'support universal background checks and a red flag law' (2026).
Jan 2026 State of the State proposed a first-in-nation law making 3-D printers block gun printing; campaign touts tougher gun laws (Aug 2026).

Signed SB 1 (Act 2) as his first bill, expanding abortion access and shielding providers and patients in state law (Mar 2023).
Signed the Reproductive Health Act (2019) and further abortion-access expansions, including a Jan 2023 bill and a June 2026 medical-records shield law.
Signed H 5595 removing restrictions on abortions after 24 weeks, leaving it to physician judgment (Aug 2026).
His Unity First PAC, launched by Moore, and his allies, spent a six-figure sum on digital ads hitting Larry Hogan's abortion record in the Senate race (Sep 2024).
Touted the abortion-access protections New York enacted under her after Dobbs; state ERA was voter-approved (Nov 2024), not signed (Jan 2026).
2026 campaign plan pledges to protect abortion access; signed 2026 laws strengthening Oregon's shield law and Planned Parenthood funding.
Told lawmakers she supports the constitutional amendment protecting reproductive freedom; also signed a right-to-contraception law (Jan-Apr 2026).
Signed a broad law codifying abortion rights (Jun 2019) and backed the 2022 Prop 5 constitutional amendment protecting reproductive liberty (2022).
Pledges to defend Amendment 79, which put abortion rights in Colorado's constitution, and state abortion-rights laws (2026 campaign).
Campaign platform pledged to enshrine reproductive care in Delaware's constitution, and he ran on an abortion-rights amendment (2024 campaign).
Vows to fight to restore abortion rights and repeal Georgia's six-week 'heartbeat' law (Apr 2026 debate; campaign site).
Health plan pledges to protect the reproductive rights codified in state law by the PRO Act (2026).
On the Roe anniversary she vowed to end Texas's abortion ban and guarantee women's right to privacy and care as governor (Jan 2026).

mctax.ev: Signed a $400 million middle-class income tax cut (cited Jan 2026).
Signed Act 46 (2024), billed as the largest income tax cut in state history; in May 2026 signed SB 3125 revising future steps but keeping most low/middle-income relief.

Signed HB 1 cutting the income tax rate from 4.4% to 3% by 2030 with a path to elimination (Mar 2025).
Budget would raise the standard deduction to $26,500 while pausing scheduled income tax rate cuts (Apr 2026).
Signed a 5% across-the-board personal income tax cut plus federal tax conformity, about $230M a year in relief (Mar 2026).
Would eliminate state income tax on up to $25,000 of tipped income (2026).

schools.ev: Campaign pledges to 'increase state support for special education' (2026); signed budget adds $193M in supplemental education grants (May 2026).
FY27 budget (Feb 2026) adds $305M to the Evidence-Based Funding formula; Aug 2026 touts raising school funding by $3 billion.
Jan 2026 State of the Commonwealth/budget proposes $159M for mandatory educator raises and higher per-pupil K-12 funding.
FY26 budget proposed a $200M foundation formula increase, largest ever, plus $33M for teacher salaries (Jan 2025 address).
Signed HB 4130, a new K-12 funding formula replacing MAEP (spring 2024); not a 2025-26 action.
Signed HB 15 (~$52M, ~3% more K-12 aid) and the STARS Act HB 252 (~$50M/yr to lift starting teacher pay) in 2025; proposed "historic $100 million" for pay (Jan 2025).
FY2026-27 budget proposes ~$2.3 billion for educators, student outcomes, and child care, raising starting teacher pay to highest in the Southeast (Apr 2026).
Jan 2025 budget proposed $60M for 2% annual increases in the K-12 funding formula; a modest raise, alongside a $44.3M ESA proposal.
Signed LB303 creating a school-finance review commission and LB645 adding $1,000/yr for teachers (Jun 2025); 2026 address backed more per-student foundation aid.

2026-27 budget address adds $565M more through the adequacy formula plus basic and special ed increases (Feb 2026).

Campaign education plan pledges to restore school funding to a constitutional level and fully implement the Fair School Funding Plan (Jul 2026).
Pledges to 'save' public schools by moving money to teacher pay, smaller classes, and special education, and to end vouchers (Oct 2026).

sen.heg: If the House impeaches Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a Senate trial decides whether to remove him; Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution was referred to committee 211–204 on Nov 10, 2026, effectively ending it this Congress.
sen.fil: Changes Senate rules so most bills can pass with a simple majority instead of 60 votes, which would let a Democratic majority move much of this agenda without Republican support.
sen.sch: Decides whether Chuck Schumer stays as leader of the Senate Democratic caucus, which shapes who sets the floor schedule and the party's strategy for the next two years.
sen.m4a: Replaces private insurance with a single public plan covering every American, ending premiums and deductibles but requiring large new federal taxes to pay for it.
sen.aca: Brings back the larger ACA marketplace subsidies that expired after 2025, lowering premiums for millions of people who buy their own coverage.
sen.medicaid: Reverses the Medicaid funding cuts and new work requirements in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, keeping coverage for people projected to lose it.
sen.drugneg: Lowers drug prices by letting Medicare negotiate many more drugs, capping insulin costs for everyone, and reining in the pharmacy benefit managers who set what patients pay.
sen.priorauth: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to approve routine care faster through electronic prior authorization, cutting delays for patients and paperwork for doctors.
sen.roe: Creates a federal right to provide and receive abortion care, overriding most state bans and restrictions passed since Roe v. Wade was overturned.
sen.gouge: Makes excessive grocery price hikes illegal and limits stores' use of personal data to charge different shoppers different prices.
sen.meat: Forces the biggest meatpackers to sell off lines of business and blocks new grocery mergers, aiming to restore competition and lower meat prices.
sen.gastax: Temporarily stops the 18.4-cent-per-gallon federal gas tax, giving drivers a modest break at the pump at the cost of highway funding.
sen.datactr: Requires data centers to cover the full cost of the power and grid upgrades they need and limits utility rate increases, so households aren't left paying for the AI boom.
sen.ctc: Makes the Child Tax Credit larger and available in full to low-income families, which cut child poverty sharply when it was temporarily expanded in 2021.
sen.childcare: Cuts child care costs, for example by capping them at 7% of family income or funding universal child care, so working parents pay far less.
sen.toptax: Undoes the 2025 tax cuts for the highest earners and closes loopholes used by billionaires, raising revenue for other priorities.
sen.pfl: Guarantees workers paid time off to care for a new child, a sick relative, or their own illness, funded through a national insurance program.
sen.downpay: Gives first-time and first-generation homebuyers federal help with a down payment, making it easier for renters to buy a home.
sen.wage: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to between $15 and $25 an hour and expands overtime pay, giving raises to millions of low-wage workers.
sen.pro: Makes it easier to form a union and harder for employers to block one, with penalties for illegal firings during organizing drives.
sen.repair: Requires equipment makers to give farmers and independent shops the tools, parts, and software needed to fix their own machines.
sen.stock: Bars members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President from trading individual stocks while in office, removing a major conflict of interest.
sen.gerry: Bans partisan gerrymandering of congressional districts nationwide, so maps can't be drawn to lock in one party's advantage.
sen.dcpr: Admits Washington, DC and Puerto Rico as states, giving their residents full voting representation in Congress and adding four senators.
sen.pacs: Gets big money out of elections by banning corporate PACs and super PACs and amending the Constitution to overturn Citizens United.
sen.termlim: Amends the Constitution to cap how long members of Congress can serve, which needs two-thirds of both chambers and approval by 38 states.
sen.imm: Overhauls the immigration system by pairing border security with a path to legal status for long-time undocumented residents.
sen.ice: Puts limits on ICE, such as no masks, body cameras, and visible ID, judicial warrants, and a right to sue, or replaces the agency altogether.
sen.isr: Puts conditions on U.S. military aid to Israel, such as limits on offensive weapons, tied to how the weapons are used in Gaza.
sen.iran: Uses the War Powers Resolution to require congressional approval for continued U.S. military action against Iran.
sen.tariff: Ends the emergency declarations behind the current tariffs and requires Congress to approve new ones, which would lower import costs for businesses and shoppers.
sen.ai: Sets federal safety and accountability rules for AI and keeps states free to pass their own protections.
sen.clean: Restores the clean-energy tax credits for solar, wind, batteries, home upgrades, and EVs that the 2025 OBBBA cut, which backers say would lower power bills by adding cheap generation.
sen.pubopt: Lets people buy into a government-run health plan or Medicare alongside private insurance, adding a lower-cost choice without ending private coverage.
sen.ssm: Rules out cuts to Social Security and Medicare benefits and has high earners pay more into them, usually by lifting the cap on wages subject to the payroll tax, to keep both funded for decades.
sen.rural: Sends more money to rural hospitals and undoes the hit they take from the 2025 Medicaid cuts, aimed at keeping emergency rooms, and maternity wards from closing.
sen.mental: Raises Medicare pay for counselors, therapists, and clinical social workers from 75% to 85% of what doctors get (S.4202, bipartisan), aimed at easing shortages, especially in rural areas, alongside stronger coverage parity.
sen.ivf: Creates a federal right to IVF and other fertility treatment and requires many insurers to cover it, protecting access after state court rulings put clinics at risk.
sen.mctax: Cuts federal income taxes for middle-class families, for example by exempting the first $75,000 of a couple's income, paid for by taxes on the wealthy.
sen.snap: Reverses the 2025 OBBBA cuts to SNAP food assistance, including its new work rules and the cost shift to states, restoring benefits for millions of people.
sen.vra: Restores the Voting Rights Act's preclearance system, so states and localities with recent voting discrimination need federal approval before changing election rules.
sen.equality: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity to federal civil-rights law, banning anti-LGBTQ discrimination in jobs, housing, public places, and federal programs.
sen.gun: Requires a background check on nearly every gun sale, including private and online sales that skip checks today.

gov.medicaid: Extends Medicaid to low-income adults in states that haven't expanded and raises payments to providers, adding coverage and helping rural hospitals stay open.
gov.drugbd: Lowers drug prices with a state board that can cap what is paid for costly drugs, limits on pharmacy benefit managers, and insulin caps.
gov.pubopt: Creates a state-backed public health plan or a path to universal coverage, giving people a lower-cost option.
gov.meddebt: Buys up and erases residents' medical debt and bars it from credit reports, so illness doesn't wreck people's ability to rent or borrow.
gov.priorauth: Ends insurer pre-approval rules for routine care and caps or eliminates insulin co-pays, speeding treatment and cutting out-of-pocket costs.
gov.aca: Uses state money to replace the federal ACA subsidies that expired after 2025, keeping marketplace premiums affordable.
gov.datactr: Makes data centers pay the full cost of the power and grid upgrades they need, or pauses new ones until rules are in place, so households don't foot the bill.
gov.utility: Holds utilities accountable with caps on fees and limits on their political influence, and freezes rates or caps power prices when bills spike.
gov.ratefreeze: Freezes utility rates or orders bill credits during an affordability emergency, giving households immediate relief on energy costs.
gov.pricecap: Pushes state regulators and the regional grid operator to cap wholesale electricity prices, limiting how much power-market spikes reach customers' bills.
gov.gastax: Cuts or suspends the state gas tax, or sends households direct payments, to offset high fuel prices.
gov.house: Builds more homes by easing zoning, speeding permits and adding supply, often with statewide rules that override local limits.
gov.eohousing: Uses executive orders and emergency powers to speed up permits and financing for housing already in the pipeline.
gov.trust: Creates dedicated funds or bonds that finance the construction of affordable homes and apartments.
gov.downpay: Gives first-time buyers help with down payments and bans renters from paying brokers' fees, lowering the upfront cost of a home or apartment.
gov.renter: Protects renters with limits on junk fees, algorithmic rent-setting, and no-cause evictions, and reins in corporate landlords buying up homes.
gov.corphome: Limits how many single-family homes large investors can buy, leaving more starter homes for families.
gov.ptaxcorp: Pays for homeowner property-tax cuts by ending tax breaks and subsidies for corporations.
gov.ptax: Cuts property taxes for homeowners, often targeted to seniors, and middle-income families, sometimes paid for by ending corporate breaks.
gov.mctax: Cuts state income taxes for middle-class families, for example through a bigger standard deduction or no tax on tips and overtime.
gov.ctc: Creates or expands a state child tax credit or earned income credit, putting cash directly into working families' pockets.
gov.sstax: Stops taxing Social Security and other retirement income, lowering taxes for seniors.
gov.millionaire: Adds a higher income tax rate on earnings above $1 million, raising revenue for housing, schools, or other priorities.
gov.prek: Offers free pre-K to every four-year-old (and sometimes three-year-olds), helping kids start school ready and saving parents child care costs.
gov.childcare: Lowers child care costs through universal child care or much larger state subsidies for working families.
gov.teacher: Raises teacher pay, such as a higher minimum starting salary, to recruit and keep teachers.
gov.vouchers: Opposes or repeals private-school voucher programs and puts that money into fully funding public schools.
gov.pfml: Creates a state insurance program that gives workers paid time off for a new child, a sick relative, or their own illness.
gov.wage: Raises the state minimum wage to $15 an hour, giving raises to the lowest-paid workers.
gov.roe: Writes the right to abortion into state law or the state constitution, protecting access regardless of federal action.
gov.ice: Limits state and local help to ICE and bars immigration arrests at schools, hospitals, courthouses, and churches without a judge's warrant.
gov.guard: Opposes a president federalizing the National Guard, or sending in another state's troops, over the governor's objection, through lawsuits, refusals, and state laws. State laws can bar other states' troops sent under Title 32, but not a president's Title 10 federalization, which only courts have checked.
gov.npv: Joins the interstate compact to award the state's electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner, which takes effect once states with 270 votes sign on.
gov.avr: Registers eligible voters automatically and passes a state voting rights act protecting access to the ballot.
gov.fraud: Overhauls oversight of state programs with surprise audits and an independent inspector general to catch fraud and waste.
gov.schools: Raises state K-12 funding or rewrites the school funding formula so districts, especially poor, and rural ones, get enough to pay teachers, and run schools.
gov.clean: Builds more clean power and adopts clean-electricity standards and home-energy rebates, which backers say will cut power bills over time.
gov.mental: Expands mental health care with crisis lines and mobile teams, more school counselors, and tougher enforcement of insurance parity.
gov.safety: Pays for more police and for community violence-intervention programs, aimed at lowering violent crime.
gov.ai: Sets state rules for AI and protects kids online, such as limits on addictive social media feeds and AI chatbots aimed at minors.
gov.college: Makes community college free, or public college tuition-free, for recent graduates, and working adults.
gov.gun: Passes gun safety laws such as universal background checks and red-flag laws that let courts take guns from people judged dangerous.
gov.tariff: Fights Trump's tariffs by suing over them, pushing back publicly and helping businesses and farmers hit by higher costs.
gov.rural: Keeps rural hospitals open with state money, higher Medicaid rates, and rural health plans.
gov.workforce: Expands apprenticeships and free job training so workers can move into better-paying jobs.

factions.Presidential Hopefuls: The 2028 draft class, and they're already running their own sets. Three of the four put distance between themselves and Trump within days of the loss (Vance flatly blamed the war; Hawley and DeSantis went after Senate leadership), while Rubio is the lone guy still setting screens for the boss.
factions.Media voices: The podcast-and-cable ecosystem that actually sets the movement's agenda, and it's splitting the fastest. Carlson declared the Trump era over and Shapiro called it a repudiation, Turning Point's Erika Kirk pointed to prices and the war but warned against infighting, and Hannity and Loomer stayed firmly in Trump's corner.
factions.Hawks: Peace-through-strength traditionalists, the wing most tied to the Iran war. Cruz called the night a Watergate-level repudiation and says the war has dragged on too long, Haley went full critic, and on Israel nobody here is giving an inch.
factions.Pragmatists and Dissenters: The told-you-so caucus of Republicans who kept Trump at arm's length all along. Christie declared "the Trump era is over," Murkowski wants Congress's war powers back, and Ayotte just showed you can survive a blue wave by running as yourself.
factions.Trump Loyalists: The franchise and its lifers. Their answer to a wipeout was promoting Stephen Miller and keeping Hegseth; even Trump's admission that the war and gas prices hurt came with an "emphatic yes" that he'd do it again. Budd, Landry, and Reeves conceded the damage without blaming him.
factions.Tea Party/Freedom Caucus: The deficit hawks and libertarian gadflies, now leading the revolt against a quick leadership vote: Ron Johnson forced a debrief meeting with Lee and Rick Scott, and Chip Roy says Republicans "dropped the ball." Rand Paul blames deficits, tariffs and the war, and Massie is pushing Hegseth impeachment articles.
factions.New Right: The post-liberal, pro-worker, anti-H-1B wing that was supposed to inherit MAGA. Banks says there's "no way to spin" the loss and wants a frank reckoning before leaders are chosen, Moreno wants a "Last Supper" lame-duck sprint, and Schmitt has stayed on offense against Democrats instead of talking about the loss.
factions.Institutionalists: The leadership class and the governors who keep the lights on. Mostly they're hedging and lining up for minority-leadership jobs (Barrasso sees "clear lessons" but names no culprit); Lankford is the outlier, calling it a referendum on Trump and ICE, while Thune and Kemp actually moved closer to the party line.

boast.John Thune: Defended the record: taxes, border, Cabinet, judges.

field.h: The 2028 field is breaking. The Cabinet isn't.
field.b: Vance (−6.3), Cruz (−4.2), Hawley (−3.9), and DeSantis (−3.3) all moved away from Trump within days. Rubio, still in the Cabinet, is the only hopeful holding with him.

iran.h: The Iran war is the position they're abandoning.
iran.b: Nine Republicans from six factions broke with the war. The only four still defending it are Trump and his inner circle: Rubio, Hegseth, and Sanders.

romney.b: Three are going harder, mostly on H-1B visas, and Chip Roy is doubling down on enforcement; only Lankford is pushing back, and only on ICE tactics. Like 2012's promised pivot, the leftward move isn't coming.

middle.b: Republicans scoring 8 or above on the Trump scale fell from 19 to 12, while those at 3 or below jumped from 5 to 13. The party is sorting away from Trump, not abandoning him.

prices.b: 17 of the 33 who gave a reason pointed to prices and cost of living; only 7 blamed Trump himself. Expect an affordability pivot, not a break with him.

tariffs.b: Three free-marketers from three factions (Cruz, Paul, Lankford) broke on tariffs, and not one Republican doubled down on them.

voices.h: The voices are outrunning the officials.
voices.b: Hosts and outside voices moved about twice as far from Trump as elected and appointed officials did, on average. The ideas tend to lead the votes.

senate.h: The Senate GOP is turning on its own leadership.
senate.b: Only 4 of the 18 Republican senators on the list have said nothing. Five pushed to delay the leadership vote, and 7 moved at least a point away from Trump; leader Thune moved toward him.

israel.b: Only Trump and Vance have shifted on Israel. The Hawks and Loyalists haven't budged from strongly pro-Israel, so the fight is at the top, not the base.

partners.h: Iran war powers is the biggest bipartisan opening.
partners.b: Nine Republicans who broke on the war map onto the Iran war powers measure, the most for any Agenda item. Tariff emergencies is next, with three.

field2.h: The 2028 field is breaking with Trump, except Rubio.
field2.b: Vance (−6.3), Cruz (−4.2), Hawley (−3.9), and DeSantis (−3.3) moved away, mostly by blaming his policies rather than him: Vance the Iran war, Cruz tariffs and the war, Hawley costs, DeSantis a do-nothing Senate. Rubio, still in the Cabinet, defended the war and holds at 10.

senate2.h: Senate Republicans want a reckoning first.
senate2.b: 14 of the 18 GOP senators on the list have now spoken, and 7 moved at least a point away from Trump, led by Lankford, Cruz, and Hawley. Johnson, Lee, Rick Scott, Budd, and Banks want a debrief before leaders are chosen. Only Thune moved toward Trump; Cotton, Schmitt, Wicker, and Tim Scott are still silent.

bipart.h: Iran, corruption, and tariffs are bipartisan openings.
bipart.b: The widest GOP breaks: the Iran war (9 Republicans across 6 factions), corruption and the Epstein files (6 across 5), and tariffs (3, with no defenders). The likeliest places for early deals.

meddebt: Signed SB 1061 keeping medical debt off consumer credit reports (Sep 2024).
house: Signed SB 79 allowing denser housing near transit (Oct 2025), on top of the 2025 CEQA streamlining laws.
ctc: Signed the 2019-20 budget creating a $1,000 credit for working families with children under six (Jun 2019).
prek: Signed the 2021-22 budget adopting universal transitional kindergarten for all 4-year-olds (Jun 2021).
pfml: Signed the 2019-20 budget expanding California's Paid Family Leave by two weeks (Jun 2019).
ice: Signed AB 49 barring immigration agents from nonpublic areas of schools without a judicial warrant (Sep 2025).
guard: Signed SB 1354 requiring his permission before other states' Guard troops enter California (Sep 2026).
roe: His campaign gave $2.1 million to Prop 1, the 2022 abortion-rights amendment, and he headlined rallies for it.
schools: Signed a $123.9B K-12 package making transitional kindergarten free for all 4-year-olds and funding school meals (Jul 2021).
clean: Signed SB 1020 setting clean-electricity targets of 90% by 2035 and 100% by 2045 (Sep 2022).
mental: Created CARE Court mental health program (2022), backed the Prop 1 behavioral health bond (2024), and signed a law expanding CARE Court (Oct 2025).
safety: Signed a retail and property crime package: felony charges for repeat theft, permanent property crimes task force (Aug 2024).
ai: Signed SB 53 frontier AI safety law, SB 243 companion-chatbot safeguards, AB 1043 app-store age checks (Sep-Oct 2025); vetoed stricter AB 1064.
college: His first budget made a second year of community college tuition-free for eligible students (Jun-Jul 2019).
gun: Signed a gun package incl. SB 2 (concealed-carry limits, stronger permit background checks) and an 11% gun and ammo tax (Sep 2023).
tariff: Announced California's lawsuit calling Trump's IEEPA tariffs unlawful, the first state to sue (Apr 2025).
rural: Signed AB 112 creating a $150M Distressed Hospital Loan Program (May 2023); aids struggling hospitals like Madera's, not rural-specific.
workforce: Executive order for a Master Plan for Career Education to widen job training and career pathways (Aug 2023).

roe: Signed the repeal of Michigan's 1931 abortion ban (Apr 2023) and the Reproductive Health Act (Nov-Dec 2023).
prek: Signed the FY25 education budget funding free pre-K for every 4-year-old (Jul 2024).
schools: Signed the FY25 education budget adding $600M to classrooms, over $400 per pupil (Jul 2024).
clean: Signed SB 271 and a climate package setting a 100% clean energy standard by 2040 (Nov 2023).
mental: FY25 education budget she signed kept $134M for student mental health and school safety, incl. $25M new (Jul 2024).
safety: Signed a budget creating a $75M Public Safety and Violence Prevention Trust Fund (Jul 2024).
ai: Signed HB 4047-4048 making it a crime to create or share nonconsensual sexual AI deepfakes (Aug 2025).
college: Signed FY25 budget guaranteeing tuition-free community college for every high school graduate (Jul 2024).
gun: Signed universal background checks and safe storage (Apr 2023) and a red-flag ERPO law, SB 83, and HB 4146-4148 (May 2023).

workforce: Signed FY27 budget with $4M for registered apprenticeships, $14.5M Going Pro and Michigan Reconnect expanded to ages 21+ (Jul 2026).
